title: Roman Abramovich re-emerged as a key intermediary
text:
IMPARTIAL NEWS + INTELLIGENT DEBATE

Account

Roman Abramovich, the former Chelsea FC owner, is acting as an unofficial go-between for Moscow and Kyiv

Roman Abramovich, the Russian billionaire and former owner of Chelsea FC, these days mostly splits his time between a luxury waterfront home in Istanbul and sailing his superyachts along the Aegean Coast.

But this glamorous lifestyle is restricted by strict sanctions imposed by the UK and other countries following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with the 59-year-old locked in expensive legal battles over his frozen assets, including funds from the Chelsea sale in that same year.

Abramovich – a close confidant of Vladimir Putin, who reportedly recommended him to Boris Yeltsin as a successor and helped select his cabinet – has now re-entered the spotlight in a key role as middleman in negotiations between the Russian president and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky.

sport

The English Football Association is set to withdraw its support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as Fifa president after he revealed plans to sell off the World Cup.

Infantino is under increasing pressure to resign and could face a vote of no confidence in the wake of now-abandoned plans to sell a ‌stake in the World Cup to private investors.

Despite walking back on his plans, Uefa has declared a loss of confidence in Infantino, with the Football Association (FA) supportive of the stance taken by European football’s governing body.

The Prime Minister said Infantino is “not the right man to lead football” and should stand down.

The FA said it was time for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”.

Uefa said Infantino had “not only lost Uefa’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.”

An emergency Fifa congress can be held as long as it is called for by 20 per cent of Fifa’s 211 member associations.A rival candidate could be put up before the November 18 deadline to take on Infantino in next March’s Fifa presidential election in Rabat, Morocco.

Ariana Grande will withdraw from public appearances and will no longer star in an upcoming musical production in London when she ends her Eternal Sunshine tour next month.Here is everything you need to know about the decision.

A representative for Grande told People that she “will be taking a step back from visibility” when her Eternal Sunshine tour ends.

It was also announced that Grande would no longer feature in a production of Sunday in the Park with George, due to play at the Barbican in 2027, with the production company saying she had their “complete understanding and support”.

Grande’s representatives said the star has faced “endless, ongoing public scrutiny”.

Grande’s reps also said she “performs a very physical show”, suggesting it may be taking a physical toll.

Her tour continues in Chicago on Monday with three dates. It will then move to London’s O2 arena for 10 dates.

Scottish researchers have teamed up with an agricultural company to explore new ways of turning a cheese byproduct into fuel.Here is how it works.

Researchers at Heriot-Watt University worked with Take Root Bio to successfully turn salty whey – a difficult, high-volume byproduct from cheese production – into a widely used fuel called bioethanol.The process could be used to tackle one of the dairy industry’s biggest waste challenges.

About 95,000 tonnes of whey is generated in the UK each year from cheese production.

Whey’s combination of milk sugars and high salt content makes management particularly difficult.

Dairy producers can generate tens of thousands of litres of whey weekly, creating environmental pressures.

Food and drink manufacturing produces a huge range of by-products, many of which still contain valuable components but can be challenging to manage.

Politics

Reform UK wants to launch “the largest military operation in the English Channel since World War Two” to stop small-boat arrivals from France.

Reform UK has said a Nigel Farage-led government would send the Royal Navy into the Channel to intercept all migrant boats there and return them to France or Belgium under a plan called “operation fortress”.

The party says the plan is in line with international law and that it will both halt small-boat arrivals and act as a humanitarian response.

Reform UK would set up a joint military command with units from the armed forces.

The armed forces would intercept unauthorised boats, detain their occupants and escort them back.

Reform UK would pass emergency legislation “as necessary” to give the joint command any further required powers.

Reform have reheated an old announcement in their latest desperate bid to distract from their growing sleaze scandals.

A Labour Party spokesperson also said “anger and easy answers won’t bring crossings down,” in response to the plan.

sport

Philippe Auclair

French football writer and broadcaster

It is not surprising that whoever is in charge of world football’s governing body should have to dine with the devil on occasion.Gianni Infantino, Fifa’s President, is following the example set by his predecessor Sepp Blatter; but if Blatter enjoyed the pomp and circumstance attached to his role, he did not actively seek out the company of the world’s most unsavoury autocrats.

Infantino hasn’t sent back the “Order of Friendship” medal Vladimir Putin pinned on his jacket at the Kremlin. He counts Rwandan de facto dictator Paul Kagame as one of his closest allies in Africa. He appears to have a penchant for populist leaders such as Narendra Modi and Javier Milei.

Explained

4 min read

Since Joe Biden lost the 2024 US presidential election, Infantino has nailed his colours to the Maga mast and his behaviour has become noticeably more erratic – culminating in this summer’s World Cup and his disastrous efforts to sell off the tournament.

Trump made himself scarce during most of the tournament played on US soil, making his sole public appearance at the final, when Infantino tried (unsuccessfully) to steer him away from the presentation of the trophy to the victorious Spanish team.

But the pair had been in touch, as was demonstrated when Trump was unable to accept the red card handed to US striker Folarin Balogun.

Trump said he had called his friend to put a stop to that nonsense; “Johnny” complied. Balogun escaped his automatic one-game suspension, triggering a furious reaction across the globe and creating a deep crack in the unity of the “football family”.

The oligarch visited Kyiv last month at Zelensky’s invitation to discuss the possibility of direct peace talks, according to Ukraine’s leader, and Putin confirmed at an economic conference in St Petersburg that he’d met with “one of the representatives of our business circles” who had been in the Ukrainian capital. Abramovich delivered the message from Zelensky to Putin that Ukraine was ready to talk, but without conceding territory it still possesses in the Donbas. Putin dismissed the offer.

Asked on the sidelines of this week’s G7 meeting whether the Russian businessman could be an intermediary, the Zelensky said, “I don’t know”, claiming that Putin “uses” people. “He has his own decisions in his head, but I know that Abramovich, when he came, I think it was very concrete, specific dialogue with him and I think he understood 100 per cent of my position … And he said that he will go and give feedback to the Kremlin, so we will see.”

Abramovich is no stranger to negotiations between Russia and Ukraine. In 2022, he was the first person on the Russian side that Zelensky’s team contacted to try to find a way of speaking to the Kremlin. While it is unclear how they first made contact, they consider him the one person they can talk to who had direct access to Putin.

Reports emerged in March 2022 that Abramovich had suffered symptoms of suspected poisoning at peace talks on the Ukraine-Belarus border, including sore eyes and peeling skin.

The recovered billionaire made a surprise appearance as a “go-between” at subsequent talks between Russian and Ukrainian negotiators in Istanbul at the end of that month. And while the negotiations failed, Abramovich remained in the picture, acting as a backchannel in negotiations over the Black Sea grain deal brokered by the United Nations several months later, which allowed Ukrainian agricultural exports to resume despite the war, according to The Wall Street Journal.

He also became an unexpected facilitator of prisoner of war exchanges between Russia and Ukraine, meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh in August 2023 to discuss the swap.

All of which makes his latest foray to Kyiv all the more intriguing. For Ukraine, Abramovich has three vital qualities it thinks could help its cause: empathy, access to Putin and the commitment to be an effective middleman. Both sides view Abramovich as an intermediary, rather than a negotiator, and he appears comfortable with this role.

While Abramovich became less prominent as Donald Trump launched his peace initiative shortly after coming to office last year, those negotiations failed to gather momentum – hence Ukraine, and perhaps Russia, trying another tack.

Ukraine is looking for a way to end the war, albeit not on Putin’s terms. Its army is more or less holding the front line and can probably carry on fighting into 2027 and beyond, but Ukrainian society is exhausted and much of the country’s energy infrastructure has been damaged by Russian bombing. There are fears that Russia could broaden its bombing campaign next winter, targeting the water supply and sewerage systems of major cities.

Even so, Ukrainians feel like they have – for the moment – gained the upper hand, in part because of their success in developing the capacity to strike military targets, oil refineries and infrastructure deep inside Russia, causing disruption and embarrassment for Putin. Russia lacks air defences to the point that Putin was so worried about the security of his Victory Day parade last month that he asked for Trump’s help in negotiating a brief ceasefire.

While Trump is distracted by Iran, both Ukraine and Russia believe that he could return to their central issue. So Zelensky has wisely demonstrated, contrary to Trump’s assertions, that he is ready to negotiate directly with Putin.

By reaching out through a middleman like Abramovich, Ukraine’s leader is also signalling to both the US and Europe that he is not the obstacle to peace.

What is less clear is why Putin let the Russian billionaire visit Zelensky in Kyiv in the first place. Perhaps he was expecting the Ukrainians to say that they were ready to give up the rest of the Donbas region and negotiate on his terms.

Putin has a track record of misreading Ukraine going back to 2004, when his clumsy efforts to install his favoured candidate as president triggered the Orange Revolution. He still believes that Russians and Ukrainians are one people, and that Ukraine’s independence is artificial.

There are those around Putin who believe that Zelensky is right and that Russia has a strong interest in ending the war. Abramovich is almost certainly among them. But Putin has dug himself into a hole and is impervious to reason. The former Chelsea owner has a challenge on his hands if he is to score his greatest tactical win.

John Lough is the head of foreign policy at the London-based New Eurasian Strategies Centre
